claim: Cortical interneurons establish inhibitory microcircuits throughout the neocortex.
source: Cortical interneurons establish inhibitory microcircuits throughout the neocortex and their dysfunction has been implicated in epilepsy and neuropsychiatric diseases.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about cortical interneurons.

claim: Cortical interneuron dysfunction has been implicated in epilepsy and neuropsychiatric diseases.
source: Cortical interneurons establish inhibitory microcircuits throughout the neocortex and their dysfunction has been implicated in epilepsy and neuropsychiatric diseases.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior literature on interneuron dysfunction.

claim: Interneurons migrate from a distal progenitor domain to populate the neocortex.
source: Developmentally, interneurons migrate from a distal progenitor domain in order to populate the neocortex – a process that occurs at a slower rate in humans than in mice.
evidence: This is established knowledge about interneuron development.

claim: Interneuron migration occurs at a slower rate in humans than in mice.
source: Developmentally, interneurons migrate from a distal progenitor domain in order to populate the neocortex – a process that occurs at a slower rate in humans than in mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on species differences in interneuron migration.

claim: Blood vessels of the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE) regulate the process of initiating interneuron migration.
source: Using embryonic mouse development as a model system, we found that the process of initiating interneuron migration is regulated by blood vessels of the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE), an interneuron progenitor domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SPARC and SerpinE1 are endothelial cell-derived paracrine factors.
source: We identified two endothelial cell-derived paracrine factors, SPARC and SerpinE1, that enhance interneuron migration in mouse MGE explants and organotypic cultures.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and western blot analysis showing expression in endothelial cells.

claim: SPARC and SerpinE1 enhance interneuron migration in mouse MGE explants and organotypic cultures.
source: We identified two endothelial cell-derived paracrine factors, SPARC and SerpinE1, that enhance interneuron migration in mouse MGE explants and organotypic cultures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from MGE explant and organotypic culture assays.

claim: Pre-treatment of human stem cell-derived interneurons (hSC-interneurons) with SPARC and SerpinE1 prior to transplantation into neonatal mouse cortex enhanced their migration in the host cortex.
source: Moreover, pre-treatment of human stem cell-derived interneurons (hSC-interneurons) with SPARC and SerpinE1 prior to transplantation into neonatal mouse cortex enhanced their migration and morphological elaboration in the host cortex.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft experimental data showing increased migratory distance.

claim: Pre-treatment of hSC-interneurons with SPARC and SerpinE1 enhanced their morphological elaboration in the host cortex.
source: Moreover, pre-treatment of human stem cell-derived interneurons (hSC-interneurons) with SPARC and SerpinE1 prior to transplantation into neonatal mouse cortex enhanced their migration and morphological elaboration in the host cortex.
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis showing longer processes and more branches.

claim: SPARC and SerpinE1-treated hSC-interneurons exhibited more mature electrophysiological characteristics compared to controls.
source: Further, SPARC and SerpinE1-treated hSC-interneurons also exhibited more mature electrophysiological characteristics compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by whole-cell recording data showing multiple electrophysiological parameters.

claim: CNS vasculature plays a critical role in regulating interneuron developmental maturation in both mice and humans.
source: Overall, our studies suggest a critical role for CNS vasculature in regulating interneuron developmental maturation in both mice and humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings in both mouse and human systems.

claim: Interneuron migration lasts days in mice.
source: The timescale for interneuron migration varies widely across species. The process lasts days in mice (Lavdas et al., 1999; Marín and Rubenstein, 2001) and several months in humans (Arshad et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Interneuron migration lasts several months in humans.
source: The timescale for interneuron migration varies widely across species. The process lasts days in mice (Lavdas et al., 1999; Marín and Rubenstein, 2001) and several months in humans (Arshad et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mouse ES-derived interneurons develop rapidly.
source: This species difference extends to stem cell-derived interneurons where mouse ES-derived interneurons develop rapidly (Au et al., 2013; Maroof et al., 2010; McKenzie et al., 2019), while human stem cell-derived interneuron (hSC-interneuron) development is protracted (Nicholas et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human stem cell-derived interneuron (hSC-interneuron) development is protracted.
source: This species difference extends to stem cell-derived interneurons where mouse ES-derived interneurons develop rapidly (Au et al., 2013; Maroof et al., 2010; McKenzie et al., 2019), while human stem cell-derived interneuron (hSC-interneuron) development is protracted (Nicholas et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The protracted development of hSC-interneurons has restricted the scope of analysis and hampered detailed functional studies.
source: Indeed, this limitation has restricted the scope of analysis on hSC-interneurons, hampering detailed functional studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known slow development of hSC-interneurons.

claim: Interneuron migration coincides with vascularization of the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE).
source: Using embryonic mouse development as a model system, we found that interneuron migration coincides with vascularization of the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE), and that by manipulating the degree of MGE vascularization in vivo, it regulates the degree of interneuron migration into the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis showing temporal correlation between vascularization and migration.

claim: Manipulating the degree of MGE vascularization in vivo regulates the degree of interneuron migration into the cortex.
source: Using embryonic mouse development as a model system, we found that interneuron migration coincides with vascularization of the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE), and that by manipulating the degree of MGE vascularization in vivo, it regulates the degree of interneuron migration into the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by data from Apcdd1 mutant mice showing altered vascularization and migration.

claim: Interneurons in mice and humans share a common vascular-based mechanism that regulates their developmental timing.
source: These data suggest that interneurons in mice and humans share a common vascular-based mechanism that regulates their developmental timing.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental findings in both species.

claim: Interneurons are generated starting ~e11 in the embryonic mouse.
source: In the embryonic mouse, this developmental process is rapid: interneurons are generated starting ~e11 and robustly migrate into the cortex by e15 (Figure 1A; Lavdas et al., 1999; Marín and Rubenstein, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Interneurons robustly migrate into the cortex by e15 in the embryonic mouse.
source: In the embryonic mouse, this developmental process is rapid: interneurons are generated starting ~e11 and robustly migrate into the cortex by e15 (Figure 1A; Lavdas et al., 1999; Marín and Rubenstein, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In human fetal development, postmitotic interneurons slowly transition to a migratory state to populate the neocortex over the course of many weeks.
source: Previous studies have found that postmitotic interneurons slowly transition to a migratory state to populate the neocortex over the course of many weeks (Arshad et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is an increase in the density of Dlx2+ interneurons in the human fetal cortex over time (15 post-conception weeks [pcw] to 22 pcw).
source: Consistent with prior reports, we observed an increase in the density of Dlx2+ interneurons in the cortex over time (15 post-conception weeks [pcw] to 22 pcw) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: There is a striking increase in vascularization of the MGE and the underlying mantle region during the time period when mouse interneuron migration initiates (e10.5 to e15.5).
source: We therefore examined the developing mouse MGE (from e10.5 to e15.5) by histology and observed a striking increase in vascularization of the MGE and the underlying mantle region during the time period when mouse interneuron migration initiates (Figure 1C,D; Daneman et al., 2009; Paredes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C,D and citations to prior literature.

claim: Vascularization of human fetal MGE slowly increased with developmental age, with robust vascularization not occurring until after 20 pcw.
source: Similarly, we found that vascularization of human fetal MGE slowly increased with developmental age, with robust vascularization not occurring until after 20 pcw (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Genetic manipulation of vascular pruning affects the number of interneurons migrating into the cortex.
source: Here, we demonstrate that not only does vascularization of mouse MGE coincide with interneuron migration, but it also plays a regulatory role since genetic manipulation of vascular pruning affects the number of interneurons migrating into the cortex.
evidence: This is supported by data from Apcdd1 mutant mice.

claim: Vascularization in the MGE is decreased in Apcdd1 GOF mice versus wildtype controls.
source: We examined MGE vessel density and average vessel size in Apcdd1 GOF (an endothelial cell-specific transgenic gain-of-function) and LOF (whole animal null) mutants at e14.5 and found that, similar to the retina and cerebellum (Mazzoni et al., 2017), vascularization in the MGE is decreased in Apcdd1 GOF and increased in Apcdd1 LOF mice versus wildtype controls (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of isolectin staining shown in Figure 1F–H.

claim: Vascularization in the MGE is increased in Apcdd1 LOF mice versus wildtype controls.
source: We examined MGE vessel density and average vessel size in Apcdd1 GOF (an endothelial cell-specific transgenic gain-of-function) and LOF (whole animal null) mutants at e14.5 and found that, similar to the retina and cerebellum (Mazzoni et al., 2017), vascularization in the MGE is decreased in Apcdd1 GOF and increased in Apcdd1 LOF mice versus wildtype controls (Figure 1F–H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of isolectin staining shown in Figure 1F–H.

claim: Fewer interneurons migrated into the cortex in Apcdd1 GOF mutants compared to wildtype controls.
source: Importantly, fewer interneurons migrated into the cortex in Apcdd1 GOF mutants, in which vascularization was less extensive compared to wildtype controls.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of calbindin+ cells shown in Figure 1I.

claim: There is a trend toward more calbindin+ migrating interneurons in Apcdd1 LOF mutants (p=0.236, paired t-test).
source: Conversely, a trend toward more calbindin + migrating interneurons were present in Apcdd1 LOF mutants (p=0.236, paired t-test) in which vessel size and density was greater (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1I, though not statistically significant.

claim: The density of endothelial cells within neural tissue is a critical regulator of interneuron migration.
source: These results suggest that the density of endothelial cells within neural tissue is a critical regulator of interneuron migration.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the Apcdd1 mutant data.

claim: Apcdd1 expression is confined to vasculature in the embryonic mouse brain.
source: To confirm that a whole animal Apcdd1 null was appropriate for analysis, we performed in situ hybridization for Apcdd1 and found that its expression is confined to vasculature in the embryonic mouse brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is a strong linear correlation between the number of migratory cells and MGE explant surface area (r2 = 0.6829).
source: Using this approach, we found a strong linear correlation between the number of migratory cells and MGE explant surface area (r2 = 0.6829) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Nearly all migratory DAPI+ cells in MGE explants are interneurons.
source: Further, we found that nearly all migratory DAPI + cells were interneurons using the Dlx6aCre driver line crossed to Ai9 in order to fate-map the migratory lineage (Monory et al., 2006; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by fate-mapping data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Interneurons from later timepoint MGE explants exhibited robust migration, whereas explants from earlier timepoints (e10.5–e12.5) had a limited capacity to migrate.
source: Consistently, we found that interneurons later timepoint MGE explants exhibited robust migration, whereas explants from earlier timepoints (e10.5–e12.5) had a limited capacity to migrate (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Early MGE explants did not significantly migrate more after the first 48 hr, even when cultured for up to a week.
source: However, even when cultured for up to a week, early explants did not significantly migrate more after the first 48 hr (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, though data is not shown.

claim: Endothelial cells produce a paracrine signal to induce interneuron migration.
source: Given the diffuse distribution of blood vessels in the MGE, the most likely mechanism is that endothelial cells produce a paracrine signal to induce interneuron migration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the distribution of blood vessels and tested experimentally.

claim: Addition of primary culture endothelial cell conditioned medium (p-EndoCM) resulted in a robust increase in interneuron migration from e11.5 MGE explants.
source: To test this directly, we prepared conditioned medium from primary cultures of embryonic brain ECs (primary culture endothelial cell conditioned medium [p-EndoCM]) and added it to e11.5 MGE explants. Consistent with our hypothesis, addition of p-EndoCM resulted in a robust increase in interneuron migration (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Conditioned medium from HBEC-5i (EndoCM) robustly increased e11.5 MGE explant migration.
source: Similar to p-EndoCM, conditioned medium from HBEC-5i (EndoCM) also robustly increased e11.5 MGE explant migration (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EndoCM significantly increased e14.5 MGE migration.
source: Interestingly, e14.5 MGE migration was also significantly increased by EndoCM (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EndoCM significantly increased the rate and overall number of interneurons that migrated into the cortex in organotypic slice cultures.
source: As with MGE explants, EndoCM also significantly increased the rate and overall number of interneurons that migrated into the cortex (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Conditioned medium from HEK 293 cells (HEK CM) did not increase MGE explant migration at either e11.5 or e14.5.
source: As a negative control, we tested the biological activity of conditioned medium from HEK 293 cells (HEK CM). HEK CM did not increase MGE explant migration at either age (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Pre-boiling EndoCM eliminated its biological activity.
source: Moreover, we found that pre-boiling EndoCM eliminated its biological activity, suggesting a protein source as a regulator of interneuron migration (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The biological activity of EndoCM was strongly reduced between 30 and 100 kDa in size fractionation experiments.
source: Finally, we size-fractionated EndoCM and found that biological activity was strongly reduced between 30 and 100 kDa (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2G.

claim: SPARC is expressed in the embryonic CNS vasculature at e14.5 MGE.
source: We examined the expression of SPARC and SerpinE1 in e14.5 MGE through publicly available expression databases (Allen Brain Atlas and GenePaint) and found that both were specifically expressed in the embryonic CNS vasculature (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SerpinE1 is expressed in the embryonic CNS vasculature at e14.5 MGE.
source: We examined the expression of SPARC and SerpinE1 in e14.5 MGE through publicly available expression databases (Allen Brain Atlas and GenePaint) and found that both were specifically expressed in the embryonic CNS vasculature (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SPARC and SerpinE1 were present in EndoCM at significantly higher levels compared to HEK292 CM.
source: We also confirmed by western blotting that SPARC and SerpinE1 were present in EndoCM at significantly higher levels compared to HEK292 CM (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Recombinant SPARC increased cell migration in MGE explants.
source: We then added recombinant SPARC or SerpinE1 to MGE explants and found that cell migration was increased, in particular with SerpinE1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Recombinant SerpinE1 increased cell migration in MGE explants, in particular more than SPARC.
source: We then added recombinant SPARC or SerpinE1 to MGE explants and found that cell migration was increased, in particular with SerpinE1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3E.

claim: A function-blocking antibody for SPARC significantly reduced the capacity of EndoCM to increase e11.5 MGE migration.
source: These reagents separately significantly reduced the capacity of EndoCM to increase e11.5 MGE migration (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A small molecule inhibitor (SK216) for SerpinE1 significantly reduced the capacity of EndoCM to increase e11.5 MGE migration.
source: These reagents separately significantly reduced the capacity of EndoCM to increase e11.5 MGE migration (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Inhibition of both SPARC and SerpinE1 does not reduce interneuron migration further than inhibiting either alone, suggesting that the two molecules may act on intersecting pathways.
source: However, inhibition of both SPARC and SerpinE1 does not reduce interneuron migration further, suggesting that the two molecules may act on intersecting pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of additive effect when both are inhibited.

claim: SPARC significantly increased the rate and overall number of interneurons that migrated into the cortex over time in organotypic slice cultures.
source: Finally, we tested whether SPARC and SerpinE1 could increase interneuron migration in an organotypic slice over time. We found that both proteins significantly increased the rate and overall number of interneurons that migrated into the cortex over time (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: SerpinE1 significantly increased the rate and overall number of interneurons that migrated into the cortex over time in organotypic slice cultures.
source: Finally, we tested whether SPARC and SerpinE1 could increase interneuron migration in an organotypic slice over time. We found that both proteins significantly increased the rate and overall number of interneurons that migrated into the cortex over time (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: p-EndoCM increased interneuron migration into the cortex in organotypic slice cultures over control.
source: We found that p-EndoCM increased interneuron migration into the cortex in organotypic slice cultures over control and that the effect was abrogated by adding SPARC function-blocking antibody and SK216 to p-EndoCM (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The effect of p-EndoCM on interneuron migration was abrogated by adding SPARC function-blocking antibody and SK216 to p-EndoCM.
source: We found that p-EndoCM increased interneuron migration into the cortex in organotypic slice cultures over control and that the effect was abrogated by adding SPARC function-blocking antibody and SK216 to p-EndoCM (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3H.

claim: hSC-interneurons migrate and mature at a slow rate, reminiscent of the protracted time frame of interneuron development in the human fetus.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that hSC-interneurons migrate and mature at a slow rate, reminiscent of the protracted time frame of interneuron development in the human fetus (Arshad et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There was a significant increase in migratory distance in hSC-interneurons treated both before and after dissociation with SPARC and SerpinE1.
source: We observed a significant increase in migratory distance in the group treated both before and afterward with SPARC and SerpinE1.
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: An even greater biological effect was observed when SPARC and Serpin were added to dissociated cells after pre-treatment.
source: Importantly, we observed an even greater biological effect when SPARC and Serpin were added to dissociated cells after pre-treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Functional maturation rate of hSC-interneurons xenografted into neonatal mouse cortex is prolonged, requiring ~7 months.
source: Previous studies have xenografted hSC-interneurons into a more functionally relevant setting: neonatal mouse cortex. They found that functional maturation rate is prolonged, requiring ~7 months (Nicholas et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: tdTomato+ hSC interneurons were almost all Dlx2+.
source: We confirmed that tdTomato + hSC interneurons were almost all Dlx2+ (Figure 4A) and also found that Combo-treated hSC-interneurons migrated significantly further than controls (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Combo-treated hSC-interneurons migrated significantly further than controls 28 days post-engraftment.
source: We confirmed that tdTomato + hSC interneurons were almost all Dlx2+ (Figure 4A) and also found that Combo-treated hSC-interneurons migrated significantly further than controls (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: At 56 days post-transplantation, SPARC/SerpinE1-treated hSC-interneurons possessed longer processes and branched more extensively.
source: At 56 days post-transplantation, we traced and analyzed the morphologies of hSC-interneurons in 3D and found that they possessed longer processes and branched more extensively (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Recordings from SPARC/SerpinE1 treatment group neurons showed significantly reduced membrane input resistance.
source: Consistent with more mature neuronal function, recordings from treatment group neurons showed significantly reduced membrane input resistance, faster membrane time constants, more hyperpolarized action potential (AP) thresholds, and increased ratios of voltage-gated sodium currents versus voltage-gated potassium currents (Figure 4E–O).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E–O.

claim: Recordings from SPARC/SerpinE1 treatment group neurons showed faster membrane time constants.
source: Consistent with more mature neuronal function, recordings from treatment group neurons showed significantly reduced membrane input resistance, faster membrane time constants, more hyperpolarized action potential (AP) thresholds, and increased ratios of voltage-gated sodium currents versus voltage-gated potassium currents (Figure 4E–O).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E–O.

claim: Recordings from SPARC/SerpinE1 treatment group neurons showed more hyperpolarized action potential (AP) thresholds.
source: Consistent with more mature neuronal function, recordings from treatment group neurons showed significantly reduced membrane input resistance, faster membrane time constants, more hyperpolarized action potential (AP) thresholds, and increased ratios of voltage-gated sodium currents versus voltage-gated potassium currents (Figure 4E–O).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E–O.

claim: Recordings from SPARC/SerpinE1 treatment group neurons showed increased ratios of voltage-gated sodium currents versus voltage-gated potassium currents.
source: Consistent with more mature neuronal function, recordings from treatment group neurons showed significantly reduced membrane input resistance, faster membrane time constants, more hyperpolarized action potential (AP) thresholds, and increased ratios of voltage-gated sodium currents versus voltage-gated potassium currents (Figure 4E–O).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4E–O.

claim: SPARC/SerpinE1-treated cells appear to have larger membrane capacitances (p=0.067).
source: Specifically, treated cells appear to have larger membrane capacitances (p=0.067), more hyperpolarized resting potentials (p=0.12), larger voltage-gated sodium currents (p=0.20), faster AP rise rates (p=0.21), narrower APs (p=0.22), and generated a greater number of APs (p=0.24) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4, though not statistically significant.

claim: SPARC/SerpinE1-treated cells appear to have more hyperpolarized resting potentials (p=0.12).
source: Specifically, treated cells appear to have larger membrane capacitances (p=0.067), more hyperpolarized resting potentials (p=0.12), larger voltage-gated sodium currents (p=0.20), faster AP rise rates (p=0.21), narrower APs (p=0.22), and generated a greater number of APs (p=0.24) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4, though not statistically significant.

claim: SPARC/SerpinE1-treated neurons may have an accelerated trajectory toward functional maturity.
source: Taken together, these electrophysiological profiles suggest that treated neurons may have an accelerated trajectory toward functional maturity.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Ablation of SPARC and SerpinE1 in immortalized or p-EndoCM reduced its capacity to increase interneuron migration.
source: Further, two EC-derived paracrine factors SPARC and SerpinE1 induce increased interneuron migration as assessed by in vitro assays. Moreover, ablation of SPARC and SerpinE1 in immortalized or p-EndoCM reduced its capacity increase in interneuron migration.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using function-blocking antibodies and inhibitors.

claim: Angiogenesis has been linked to pathfinding during interneuron tangential migration.
source: Our findings support previous studies that have linked angiogenesis to pathfinding during interneuron tangential migration (Barber et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018) and MGE mitosis (Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Angiogenesis has been linked to MGE mitosis.
source: Our findings support previous studies that have linked angiogenesis to pathfinding during interneuron tangential migration (Barber et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018) and MGE mitosis (Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Radial glia in the MGE undergo a transition during embryonic development where their pial endfeet detach and connect to MGE vasculature.
source: Further, radial glia in the MGE undergo a transition during embryonic development where their pial endfeet detach and connect to MGE vasculature (Tan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SPARC expression is significantly enriched in brain endothelial cells versus other endothelial populations (log2-fold increase 3.97).
source: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) in mouse indicates that SPARC expression is significantly enriched in brain endothelial cells versus other endothelial populations (log2-fold increase 3.97) (Hupe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SerpinE1 expression increases in mouse brain endothelial cells, peaking at e14.5.
source: In the same study, SerpinE1 expression increases in mouse brain endothelial cells, peaking at e14.5, which coincides with the timepoint where we observe robust migration in MGE explants.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and correlation with experimental observations.

claim: SPARC is expressed in human endothelial cells.
source: Both SPARC (Butler et al., 2016; Girard and Springer, 1995; Sage et al., 1989) and SerpinE1 (Canfield et al., 1989) are expressed in human endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SerpinE1 is expressed in human endothelial cells.
source: Both SPARC (Butler et al., 2016; Girard and Springer, 1995; Sage et al., 1989) and SerpinE1 (Canfield et al., 1989) are expressed in human endothelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The maturation of CNS vasculature may regulate the timing of human fetal interneurons migration.
source: We found that hSC-interneurons exhibit greater migration and faster functional maturation when treated with vascular factors, SPARC and SerpinE1, suggesting that the maturation of CNS vasculature may similarly regulate the timing of human fetal interneurons migration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the experimental findings with hSC-interneurons.

claim: During human fetal development, both SPARC and SerpinE1 are expressed at low levels in subpallium at 8 and 9 pcw.
source: During human fetal development, both SPARC and SerpinE1 are expressed at low levels in subpallium at 8 and 9 pcw, and both peak in their expression in the cortex between 37 pcw and 1 year of age (Allen Institute BrainSpan Database, Developmental Transcriptome, https://www.brainspan.org/rnaseq/search/index.html).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a public database.

claim: Both SPARC and SerpinE1 peak in their expression in the human cortex between 37 pcw and 1 year of age.
source: During human fetal development, both SPARC and SerpinE1 are expressed at low levels in subpallium at 8 and 9 pcw, and both peak in their expression in the cortex between 37 pcw and 1 year of age (Allen Institute BrainSpan Database, Developmental Transcriptome, https://www.brainspan.org/rnaseq/search/index.html).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a public database.

claim: The MGE (also known as the germinal matrix) is the primary site of periventricular hemorrhages in prematurely born babies.
source: Further, the MGE (also known as the germinal matrix) is the primary site periventricular hemorrhages in prematurely born babies (Luo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Periventricular hemorrhages in the MGE are hypothesized to be due to newly formed (and thus weaker) vasculature in the MGE during the third trimester.
source: It has been hypothesized that this is due to newly formed (and thus weaker) vasculature in the MGE during the third trimester (Ballabh et al., 2004; Ballabh et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The timing of vascularization, which is the source of SPARC and SerpinE1 in the MGE, may help to coordinate species-specific aspects of neuronal maturation.
source: As such, it is an appealing possibility that the timing of vascularization, which we posit to be the source of SPARC and SerpinE1 in the MGE, helps to coordinate species-specific aspects of neuronal maturation.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Delayed vascularization in humans may serve a regulatory role in delaying interneuron migration until pyramidal neurons have achieved sufficient maturity to allow for interneuron circuit integration.
source: Here, delayed vascularization in humans may serve a regulatory role in delaying interneuron migration until pyramidal neurons have achieved sufficient maturity to allow for interneuron circuit integration.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional significance of delayed vascularization.

claim: SPARC has been implicated in cell differentiation.
source: SPARC has been implicated in cell differentiation (Hrabchak et al., 2008; Stary et al., 2005) and migration (Arnold and Brekken, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SPARC has been implicated in cell migration.
source: SPARC has been implicated in cell differentiation (Hrabchak et al., 2008; Stary et al., 2005) and migration (Arnold and Brekken, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SPARC is correlated with increased cancer metastasis.
source: SPARC is also correlated with increased cancer metastasis and its increased expression in cancer stromal cells results in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition by downregulation of E-cadherin and upregulation of N-cadherin (Nagaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Increased expression of SPARC in cancer stromal cells results in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition by downregulation of E-cadherin and upregulation of N-cadherin.
source: SPARC is also correlated with increased cancer metastasis and its increased expression in cancer stromal cells results in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition by downregulation of E-cadherin and upregulation of N-cadherin (Nagaraju et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SPARC can influence migration through integrins and integrin-linked kinases.
source: SPARC can influence migration through integrins and integrin-linked kinases (Thomas et al., 2010) and by modulating the activity of matrix metalloproteases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SPARC can influence migration by modulating the activity of matrix metalloproteases.
source: SPARC can influence migration through integrins and integrin-linked kinases (Thomas et al., 2010) and by modulating the activity of matrix metalloproteases.
evidence: This is supported by general knowledge about SPARC function.

claim: Integrin signaling regulates interneuron migration during development.
source: Indeed integrin signaling also regulates interneuron migration during development (Stanco et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SerpinE1 is implicated in cell migration through the uPA/urokinase pathway.
source: SerpinE1 (also known as plasminogen activator inhibitor-1) is also implicated in cell migration through the uPA/urokinase pathway (Grøndahl-Hansen et al., 1993; Mahmood et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The urokinase pathway has been linked to interneuron tangential migration by acting through the c-Met receptor and hepatocyte growth factor.
source: The urokinase pathway has been linked to interneuron tangential migration by acting through the c-Met receptor and hepatocyte growth factor (Powell et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SPARC functions at the interface between cells and ECM as a matricellular protein.
source: As a matricellular protein, SPARC functions at the interface between cells and ECM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SPARC.

claim: Reduced collagen levels are observed in SPARC null mice.
source: Reduced collagen levels are observed in SPARC null mice and there is compelling evidence that SPARC reduces cell adhesion to ECM, enabling an intermediate state of adhesion that is conducive to migration (DiMilla et al., 1991; Palecek et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SPARC reduces cell adhesion to ECM, enabling an intermediate state of adhesion that is conducive to migration.
source: Reduced collagen levels are observed in SPARC null mice and there is compelling evidence that SPARC reduces cell adhesion to ECM, enabling an intermediate state of adhesion that is conducive to migration (DiMilla et al., 1991; Palecek et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SerpinE1 modulates ECM by binding to vitronectin.
source: SerpinE1 also modulates ECM by binding to vitronectin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SerpinE1 function.

claim: SerpinE1 binding to vitronectin interferes with vitronectin binding to integrin αV, resulting in greater integrin αV-fibronectin binding and reduced cell adhesion.
source: This interferes with its binding to integrin αV, resulting in greater integrin αV-fibronectin binding and reduced cell adhesion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SerpinE1 mechanism.

claim: The balance between integrin αV interactions with vitronectin and fibronectin helps to regulate neural stem cell self-renewal versus differentiation.
source: In the context of neural stem cells, the balance between integrin αV interactions with vitronectin and fibronectin helps to regulate self-renewal versus differentiation (Dai et al., 2016; Varun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vitronectin has a role in regulating differentiation in cerebellar granule precursors.
source: Vitronectin has a similar role in regulating differentiation in cerebellar granule precursors (Hashimoto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: SPARC and SerpinE1 act by tipping the balance toward cell differentiation and migration.
source: Taken together, we hypothesize that SPARC and SerpinE1 act by tipping the balance toward cell differentiation and migration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings and known mechanisms.

claim: Human ventral telencephalic organoids require ~14 days pre-treatment with SPARC and SerpinE1 before enhanced migration can be detected in vitro.
source: Of note, we empirically determined that human ventral telencephalic organoids require ~14 days pre-treatment with SPARC and SerpinE1 before we could detect enhanced migration in vitro.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The requirement for 14 days pre-treatment may reflect a human-specific difference in responding to endothelial cues compared with mouse interneurons that operate under a more compressed timescale.
source: This may reflect a human-specific difference in responding to endothelial cues compared with mouse interneurons that operate under a more compressed timescale.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental observation.

claim: Migration of hSC-interneurons into host mouse cortex occurs at a slow rate over 7 months.
source: In fact, this may account for previous observations by Nicholas and colleagues that migration of hSC-interneurons into host mouse cortex occurs at a slow rate over 7 months (Nicholas et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Host vascularization of xenografts has been shown to occur over a period of months.
source: This may be explained by host vascularization of the xenograft, which has been shown to occur over a period of months (Mansour et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Pre-treatment with SPARC and SerpinE1 allows xenografts to bypass host vascularization as a means to trigger migration.
source: We hypothesize that pre-treatment with SPARC and SerpinE1 allows our xenograft to bypass host vascularization as a means to trigger migration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the experimental findings.

claim: Pre-treatment may prime hSC-interneurons to more rapidly integrate and mature into the host cortex.
source: Therefore, pre-treatment may prime hSC-interneurons to more rapidly integrate and mature into the host cortex.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings.

claim: Levels of SPARC and SerpinE1 were detected at low levels in the mouse MGE at e14.5.
source: Of note, we found that levels of SPARC and SerpinE1 were detected a low levels in the mouse MGE at e14.5 (data not shown), consistent with in situ hybridization from Allen Institute and GenePaint (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations and public database data.

claim: The higher levels of SPARC and SerpinE1 used to elicit a biological effect in hSC-interneurons compared to endogenous levels is due to context differences between culture and embryonic microenvironment.
source: We hypothesize that this is due to context. In culture, SPARC and SerpinE1 are added to the medium and must diffuse through Matrigel-embedded organoids to reach hSC-interneurons. This is in contrast to the embryonic microenvironment in which vasculature is in close contact with interneuron progenitors, and this configuration likely enhances the effects of SPARC and SerpinE1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the difference in effective concentrations.

claim: Employing SPARC and SerpinE1 in a bioengineered vascular microenvironment could potentially amplify the effects demonstrated in this study.
source: A number of studies have utilized bioengineering to recapitulate the vascular microenvironment (Raghavendran et al., 2016; Shirure et al., 2017). Employing SPARC and SerpinE1 in such a context could potentially amplify the effects we demonstrated in this study.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for future work based on prior bioengineering studies.

claim: Pre-treated hSC-interneurons exhibit more maturity in vitro, suggesting SPARC/SerpinE1 treatment may be effective when applied to organoid and monolayer approaches.
source: Moreover, our pre-treated hSC-interneurons also exhibit more maturity in vitro, suggesting SPARC/SerpinE1 treatment may also be effective when applied to organoid and monolayer approaches.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vitro migration data.

claim: Paracrine cues derived from ECs may regulate the development of other neuronal populations.
source: Finally, consistent with previous work (Karakatsani et al., 2019), paracrine cues derived from ECs may similarly regulate the development of other neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior literature and the current findings.

claim: This study may serve as a general strategy for inducing hSC-neuron functional maturation in other neuronal cell types such as pyramidal neurons.
source: As such, our study may well serve as a general strategy for inducing hSC-neuron functional maturation in other neuronal cell types such as pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Apcdd1 is a negative regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling.
source: Apcdd1, a negative regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, is critical for CNS vascular development and blood-brain barrier maturation (Shimomura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Apcdd1 is critical for CNS vascular development and blood-brain barrier maturation.
source: Apcdd1, a negative regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling, is critical for CNS vascular development and blood-brain barrier maturation (Shimomura et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.
